lead: On the Sunday of the Visitation of Mary, Mother of God, to Elizabeth, the Suboro season moves from Nazareth to the hill country of Judea. The evening Gospel already tells of the meeting (Luke 1:39–45). The Old Testament lessons gather women through whom God worked: Rebekah at the well, who runs to serve a stranger and is chosen to carry the promise (Genesis 24:15–27); Hannah, who sings when God gives her a son (1 Samuel 2:1–11); the capable woman whose “strength and dignity are her clothing” (Proverbs 31:25); and Isaiah's promise that the deaf will hear and “the meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord” (Isaiah 29:19). The Catholic Epistle calls the Church “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).

The three readings studied here form one song. Hannah sings of the God who lifts up the poor; Paul proclaims the God who “desires everyone to be saved” through one mediator; Mary, carrying that mediator in her womb, sings Hannah's song again in a new key. Visit, joy and praise are the key words of this Sunday.

set: Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah, and she had no children. Year after year at the shrine of Shiloh she wept, and she prayed so intensely that the priest Eli thought she was drunk (1 Samuel 1:12–14). God heard her, and she bore Samuel. When the child was weaned she brought him to Shiloh and gave him to the Lord. Her song is her response.

Many scholars think the song was an older hymn of Israel, placed on Hannah's lips because it fits her story. It ends with a king and an “anointed one” (v. 10), though Israel had no king yet; it looks forward to David, and beyond him to the Messiah.
str: v. 1: Hannah's joy: “My heart exults in the Lord”.
vv. 2–3: there is no Holy One like the Lord; a warning to the proud.
vv. 4–8: the great reversals: the mighty broken, the feeble strengthened; the barren bears seven; the poor raised from the dust.
vv. 9–10: the Lord guards his faithful, judges the earth and strengthens his anointed.
v. 11: Elkanah goes home; the boy Samuel stays to serve the Lord.
kw: In v. 1, “my strength is exalted” is literally “my horn is lifted up”, an image from a wild ox raising its horns. The same word returns in v. 10, “the power of his anointed”. Zechariah's song uses it for Christ, the “horn of salvation” (Luke 1:69, NRSV “a mighty savior”).
A title of God in the Psalms and Deuteronomy: firm, safe, unchanging. The POC renders it “a sure refuge”.
The first time in the Bible that a king is called God's anointed. In Greek this is christos. Hannah's song, at the beginning of the books of Samuel, already points to the Messiah.
vv: Hannah prayed and said, “My heart exults in the Lord; my strength is exalted in my God.
Hannah's prayer begins with joy in God himself, not first in the gift. Mary will begin the same way: “my spirit rejoices in God my Savior”.
He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.
The ash heap outside a town was where beggars and lepers sat. God's way is to turn the world's order upside down. Psalm 113:7–8 repeats these words almost exactly.
The Lord will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king, and exalt the power of his anointed.
ch: The Catechism names Hannah, the mother of Samuel, among the holy women of the Old Covenant whose mission prepared for that of Mary (CCC 489). Many Fathers and later commentators have noticed how closely Mary's Magnificat follows Hannah's song: the joy in God, the lowly lifted up, the hungry filled, the proud brought down. In Hannah, a barren woman who gives her long-awaited son to God, the Church sees a figure of Mary who offers her Son, and of the Church who rejoices in the God who lifts up the poor.

r.h: God desires everyone to be saved
set: In the First Letter to Timothy, Paul instructs his co-worker, who leads the church at Ephesus, on the order of community life. Chapter 2 begins with a call to pray “for everyone, for kings and all who are in high positions” (2:1–2). Today's verses give the reason: the God to whom we pray wants all to be saved. Then Paul speaks of how men and women should pray and present themselves in the assembly.
str: v. 4: God's will: everyone saved, everyone knowing the truth.
vv. 5–6: a short creed: one God, one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
v. 7: Paul appointed herald, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles.
v. 8: men are to pray with holy hands lifted up, without anger.
vv. 9–10: women are to adorn themselves with modesty and good works, not with costly display.
kw: One who stands between two parties to reconcile them. Christ can be the one mediator because he is both God and “himself human”.
The only place this form is found in the New Testament. It echoes Jesus' own words: the Son of Man came “to give his life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Here Paul says “for all”.
Related to kosmos (order, ornament). True adornment is an ordered life, shown in good works.
vv: who desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
This verse is the reason for praying for everyone, even rulers who persecute. No one lies outside God's saving desire.
For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human,
“One God” is the faith of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4). “One mediator” is the faith of the Church. Christ's mediation does not compete with anyone; it makes room for others to share in it.
I desire, then, that in every place the men should pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument;
Standing with lifted hands was the common posture of prayer for Jews and early Christians. Prayer and quarrelling do not go together.
but with good works, as is proper for women who profess reverence for God.
The point of vv. 9–10 is not a dress code but where beauty is found. Mary, the handmaid of the Lord, is the model of a woman adorned with faith and service.
ch: The Catechism quotes 2:4 to show that God wants all to be saved and to know the truth, which is why the Church is missionary (CCC 74, 851). On the one mediator, the Second Vatican Council teaches that Mary's maternal role “in no way obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ, but rather shows its power”; it flows from Christ's merits and depends entirely on him (Lumen Gentium 60; CCC 970). Mary at the Visitation is the clearest picture of this: she brings Christ to Elizabeth, and all the joy comes from him.

set: Right after the Annunciation, Mary goes to visit Elizabeth, whose pregnancy the angel had given her as a sign (1:36). Luke does not name the town; an ancient tradition places it at Ein Karem, a few kilometres west of Jerusalem. From Nazareth that is a journey of several days.

Luke tells the story with echoes of 2 Samuel 6, when King David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); Elizabeth asks, “why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” David danced before the ark; John leaps in the womb. The ark stayed in the house of Obed-edom three months (2 Samuel 6:11); Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months. Several Fathers and many Catholic commentators see Mary as the new ark, carrying God's presence.
str: vv. 39–40: the journey and the greeting.
vv. 41–45: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses Mary and her child and praises her faith.
vv. 46–50: the Magnificat, first part: what God has done for Mary.
vv. 51–55: second part: what God does for his people: reversals, mercy, the promise to Abraham.
v. 56: Mary stays about three months and returns home.
kw: Not nervous hurry but eager readiness. The Greek word also carries the sense of zeal. Love does not delay.

The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22). Here the child leaps not in struggle but “for joy” (v. 44). John begins his mission as forerunner before he is born.
To make great, to declare great. Mary cannot make God greater; she makes his greatness known. The Latin first word, Magnificat, gives the song its name.
Humble condition, low estate. God looks on what the world overlooks, as he looked on Hannah's misery (1 Samuel 1:11).
vv: When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit
Mary speaks, and the Spirit comes. Where Mary brings Christ, the Holy Spirit fills hearts with joy.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
“My Lord” is the title the Old Testament gives to God and to the Messiah king (Psalm 110:1). Elizabeth is the first to call Mary, in effect, Mother of God.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.”
Mary's first blessedness is her faith. Jesus himself will say the same: blessed are those who hear the word of God and obey it (11:28).
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
A prophecy fulfilled every time the Church sings to Mary or prays the Hail Mary.
ch: The Catechism notes that John was “filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb” and that the Visitation was a visit of God to his people (CCC 717). Elizabeth's greeting, joined to Gabriel's, forms the first part of the Hail Mary (CCC 2676). The Magnificat is “the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church” (CCC 2619), and the words “all generations will call me blessed” are the foundation of the Church's devotion to Mary (CCC 971).

St Ambrose, commenting on this Gospel, wished that the soul of Mary might be in each believer to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each to rejoice in God (in substance). The Magnificat is not only Mary's song but the song of every lowly person whom God has visited.

qa: If Christ is the “one mediator”, why do we ask Mary to pray for us?

Because her prayer, like the prayers we ask of one another, depends entirely on Christ and leads to him. The Church teaches that Mary's role shows the power of Christ's mediation rather than diminishing it (Lumen Gentium 60; CCC 970). At the Visitation she brings Christ, and Elizabeth is filled with the Spirit.
Did Mary herself compose the Magnificat?

Luke presents it as Mary's song, and the Church prays it as hers. It is woven from the Psalms and Hannah's song, the prayers a devout young woman of Israel would know by heart. Mary prays the Scriptures and makes them her own.
Why does the Magnificat speak of the mighty brought down? Is it a political song?

It speaks of God's way of acting in history, which overturns pride and lifts up the lowly. It is not a call to hatred but a warning to the proud and a hope for the poor, and it calls the Church to share God's care for the poor (CCC 2448).
rite: The Malankara faithful have a deep love for St Mary, the Mother of God, shown in many prayers and in the fast of the first eight days of September before the feast of her birth. On this Sunday the Church sees in Mary the model of the one who receives Christ and at once goes out to serve. In the Holy Qurbono we receive the same Lord whom Mary carried to Elizabeth; the Visitation teaches us to carry him from the altar into the homes of the sick, the elderly and the lonely. As the Suboro season moves toward Yaldo, many Malankara families prepare by prayer and fasting, so that their hearts, like Elizabeth's house, may be ready to welcome him.
study: Hannah and Mary both begin with joy in God himself, not first in his gifts. What would it mean for my prayer to begin there?
1 Timothy 2:4 says God desires everyone to be saved. For whom, outside my circle, should I pray this week?
Mary went “with haste” to serve. Who is the Elizabeth near me, waiting for a visit?
Which line of the Magnificat do I most need to make my own in this Suboro season, on the way to Yaldo?
